title: Compression overhead for adversarial robustness
formal: Is there a universal constant \(K>0\) such that the following implication holds for every nonempty domain \(X\), every nonempty total binary concept class \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension, every integer \(k\ge1\), and every perturbation map \(U:X\to2^{X}\) satisfying \(x\in U(x)\)? If \(\mathcal C\) admits an ordinary labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(k\), must it admit an adversarially robust labeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(\lceil Kk\rceil\)? The constant is independent of the class, domain, perturbation sets and sample length. Perturbation sets may be infinite. This makes the size-overhead assertion in Open Problem 28 explicit, with \(k\) denoting the available ordinary compression bound.
why: Sample compression asks how much of a training set determines a predictor consistent with all its constraints. Adversarial robustness replaces each example by an entire set of required predictions. A constant-overhead theorem would connect these two information requirements without charging separately for the number of possible perturbations.
status_note: Open Problem 28 in the ALT 2025 source. A bounded later-work search and the author bibliography checked on 2026-09-14 did not reveal a matching resolution. importance.reason: A structural transfer question between ordinary and adversarially robust sample compression, testing whether robustness imposes information overhead independent of perturbation-set size; more general than a bound for one attack family.

sentences: The question asks whether ordinary sample compression can be made adversarially robust with only a universal constant factor in size.
A message contains original labeled examples and a counted auxiliary bitstring.
The reconstructed predictor must label every allowed perturbation correctly whenever the full sample is robustly realizable.
Known reductions impose a perturbation-cardinality factor or a stability assumption on the ordinary scheme.
The general question permits infinite perturbation sets and asks whether that overhead can be avoided.

definitions:
A sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\) is any finite sequence of points of \(X\) with labels in \(\{0,1\}\), including the empty sequence. A labeled compression scheme consists of fixed deterministic maps \(\kappa,\rho\). The compressor sends \(S\) to \((T,b)\), where \(T\) is a finite ordered sequence of labeled examples drawn from \(S\) and \(b\) is a finite binary string. Following the source's sequence convention, every entry of \(T\) must occur in \(S\); reordering or repetition is allowed, and every retained occurrence is counted. Size at most \(k\) means \(|T|+|b|\le k\) on every sample. The reconstructor maps only \((T,b)\) to a total binary predictor \(\rho(T,b):X\to\{0,1\}\). It does not receive the omitted examples, their original indices, or the original sample length for free. One labeled example counts as one unit regardless of its representation length; each auxiliary bit also counts as one unit. No computability or running-time restriction is imposed.

Ordinary realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(x_i)=y_i\) for every \(i\). An ordinary scheme must reconstruct a predictor satisfying those equalities for every realizable sample. Robust realizability means that some \(c\in\mathcal C\) satisfies \(c(z)=y_i\) for every sample position \(i\) and every \(z\in U(x_i)\). A robust scheme must have \(\rho(\kappa(S))(z)=y_i\) for all these positions and perturbations whenever the sample is robustly realizable. The compressed examples must be original labeled examples, not freely chosen perturbed points. Each pair of maps may depend on \(\mathcal C\) and, in the robust case, on the entire fixed map \(U\), but is selected once for all samples. Reconstructed predictors can lie outside \(\mathcal C\). There is no correctness requirement on nonrealizable samples, although the size bound still applies. Empty samples impose no correctness constraints.

A finite set is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if all its binary labelings are restrictions of members of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the supremum of the cardinalities of shattered finite sets; it is required to be finite.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the universal constant-overhead implication, or a proof that no universal \(K\) works. A negative answer must establish ordinary compression of size \(k\) for its finite-VC class and a robust compression requirement exceeding \(\lceil Kk\rceil\), for arbitrarily large proposed constants \(K\); nonexistence of any bounded robust scheme for such a class also suffices. Bounds depending on perturbation-set size, or a conclusion for stable ordinary schemes alone, do not establish this implication.

context_blocks.text: The source writes the available ordinary size as a function of VC dimension. Here the available bound is called k so that the constant hidden in its proposed overhead is explicitly universal. The printed phrase that the domain has a compression scheme is read as referring to the concept class; sample compression is a property of a class together with its reconstructor.

The decoder knows the fixed perturbation map, but it must recover a predictor from original examples and auxiliary bits. Retaining one original example does not by itself identify which of its potentially many perturbations an ordinary compressor selected. This distinction is part of the information requirement, even when computation is unrestricted.

For uniformly finite perturbation sets, Theorem 26 gives an additional logarithmic dependence on their maximum cardinality. Theorem 27 removes this factor under the stronger premise of a stable ordinary compression scheme. Stability requires that discarding unselected examples leave the compressor’s message unchanged.

Theorem 29 establishes that robust learnability alone need not give a bounded robust compression scheme. Its construction starts from a partial concept class. It does not supply the ordinary bounded-compression premise for the resulting total class required here; it is therefore not a resolution of Open Problem 28.
